argument: Sartre argues that the meaning we see in everyday things - words, chairs, dinner rituals, even our own identities - is not built into those things by some cosmic order, but is added by human beings, a condition he calls the absurdity of the world. Because no God has preordained an essence for people the way Plato and Aristotle thought essences existed for objects, existence precedes essence: we exist first, without a fixed nature, and only afterward determine through our choices what we become. This makes us radically free and fully responsible - 'condemned to be free' - and the central failure Sartre diagnoses is bad faith: the convenient, self-serving lie people tell themselves (like the waiter who insists he has no other options) to avoid facing how much choice they actually have.
keyIdeas: Sartre's 'absurdity of the world' names the strangeness that appears when familiar things - a repeated word, a houseplant, an ordinary dinner - are stripped of the meaning we habitually project onto them, revealing that meaning isn't inherent to the things themselves.

Building on Husserl's phenomenology and Hume's critique of causation (the pool-ball example), Sartre holds that even basic structures like cause and effect are meanings humans impose on raw experience, not features discovered in the world itself.

Against the essentialist view (Plato, Aristotle) that objects and people have a fixed, predetermined nature, Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' means a person exists first and only later determines, through their choices, what they will be.

'Man is condemned to be free': we never chose to exist, yet once we exist we are fully responsible for everything we choose within that freedom - a condition Kierkegaard describes as producing dread, which people try to escape by being 'lost in the infinite' (endless deliberation) or 'lost in the finite' (simply copying others).

Bad faith is accepting a belief not because it's the most convincing one, but because it's convenient and lets a person avoid an uncomfortable truth about their own freedom - illustrated by the waiter who insists he 'has always been a waiter' to avoid admitting he is choosing not to consider other options.

terms.def: Sartre's term for the strangeness revealed when the meaning humans habitually attach to ordinary things is stripped away, showing that meaning is added, not inherent.
Husserl's project of studying raw experience by trying to strip away all humanly imposed meanings and categories, so as to study phenomena as they actually are.
The Platonic and Aristotelian idea that objects and people have a fixed, defining nature (essence) that exists prior to and independent of them.
Sartre's core existentialist claim: there is no fixed nature placed in a person before birth; a person exists first and only afterward determines, through choices, what they will be.
Sartre's phrase for the fact that we never chose to exist, yet once we do exist we are fully responsible for everything we choose.
Accepting a belief not because it is the most convincing one, but because it is convenient and lets a person avoid an uncomfortable truth, especially about their own freedom and choices.
